evals.prompt:
Use ONLY the control list below to judge overlap with the existing corpus — not the live risk-map/yaml/controls.yaml, which changes over time (per ADR-033 Amendment 2026-07-30, this is a pinned eval fixture, not corpus content):

- controlToolCredentialLifecycleManagement — issue, rotate, and revoke credentials granted to agent tool integrations, scoping credential lifetime to the session or task that requested them so a credential does not remain valid after the agent's task concludes.
- controlAgentActionAuthorizationGating — require an explicit authorization decision (human or policy engine) before an agent executes a high-consequence action.
- controlModelOutputProvenanceLabeling — attach provenance metadata to model-generated output so downstream consumers can distinguish it from human-authored content.
- controlDataRetentionScheduling — enforce a defined retention and deletion schedule for stored data, including agent-collected data.
- controlThirdPartyToolVettingProcess — vet and approve third-party tools before they are made available for agent invocation.
- controlAgentReasoningTraceLogging — capture the agent's reasoning trace (not just the actions taken) for later audit and incident reconstruction.

Stress-test this draft control:

Title: Agent Tool Invocation Allowlisting
Description: Restrict an agent to invoking only tools whose identity is cryptographically verified against an explicit, pre-registered allowlist, denying by default any call to a tool that is absent from the list or whose signature does not match its registered entry. The allowlist and its signing trust root are stored in an admin-controlled store separate from the tool registry itself, so compromising the registry alone cannot forge a passing signature. Identity here means a signed manifest or publisher-attested identifier, not a display name or free-text description — a lookalike name, a typosquatted tool, or a tampered registry entry fails the signature check even if its name matches an allowlisted entry. This bounds which tools an agent can reach at all; it does not evaluate the legitimacy of a specific invocation of an already-allowlisted tool — that is the concern of per-action authorization controls, not this one.
Personas: personaAgenticProvider, personaApplicationDeveloper
Components: componentTools, componentOrchestrationInputHandling
Risks: riskToolSourceProvenance, riskToolRegistryTampering, riskRogueActions
Mappings: nist-ai-rmf: [MEASURE-2.7@1.0]
Counterfactuals: considered blocklisting known-bad tools instead; rejected because default-allow leaves any newly added malicious tool unblocked until discovered. Considered folding this into controlAgentActionAuthorizationGating (fixture); rejected because that control governs a human/policy-engine authorization decision for a specific high-consequence action at the moment it's attempted, while this control is a static, coarser-grained membership check on tool identity performed before any action-level decision is even reached — a tool that fails this gate never gets to the point where an authorization decision would be evaluated. Considered folding this into controlThirdPartyToolVettingProcess (fixture); rejected because vetting is a one-time, pre-availability approval process applied when a tool is onboarded, while this control is an ongoing, per-invocation runtime signature check applied on every call attempt. Considered listing only riskToolSourceProvenance and riskRogueActions; added riskToolRegistryTampering because the signature check is, on its own mechanism, exactly the runtime integrity monitoring against a known-good baseline that risk's text calls for — because it runs on every call, it also detects tampering after vetting — the post-vetting-compromise case that risk specifically describes. riskToolSourceProvenance is kept as the lead risk (its text names the tool shadowing/typosquatting/schema poisoning attack patterns this mechanism is built against), riskToolRegistryTampering as a second, equally-direct risk, and riskRogueActions as the downstream/cascading risk per riskToolSourceProvenance's own "typically manifests as riskRogueActions" language. NIST AI RMF MEASURE-2.7 chosen following the corpus precedent of controlComponentIdentityProvenance, an identity/integrity-verification control mapped to the same subcategory for the same reason (runtime verification of an invocation-time identity claim) — not the mapping-selection skill's least-privilege/permission-scoping worked example, which is a different control shape than this one. componentOrchestrationInputHandling chosen over componentTools alone because its edge (to: componentTools) places it as the actual dispatch gate between a tool-call decision and the external tool, not just the destination the call lands on.
evals.expected_output: Applies the lenses against the fixture (for control overlap) and the real risks.yaml/controls.yaml/components.yaml/personas.yaml (for risk-linkage, mapping-precedent, and scope precision) and finds the control's premise sound — the enforcement point is real, the mechanism is well-grounded, the three risks are each individually defensible, and the counterfactuals against the two closest fixture entries are genuine, not strawmen — but surfaces specific, well-evidenced gaps in how precisely the draft's efficacy claims are scoped (e.g. whether the mechanism defends a compromised-publisher-key case as well as a registry-tampering case, whether the persona list covers the parties the linked risks name, such as the platform operator of the trust-root store, whether the description's text is placed in the right field under the control description/guidance design record, risk-map/docs/design/control-description-and-guidance.md: the description carries mechanism — cryptographic signature verification, the separate admin-controlled trust-root store, signed-manifest identity — that belongs in `guidance` (DG5), a negated means ('not a display name or free-text description', DG3), and a closing sentence that defines the control by contrast with per-action authorization controls, which belongs in the boundary section of `guidance` (DG4)). This is a well-formed but underspecified draft, not a duplicate and not a broken premise: verdict NEEDS-WORK, not RETHINK, and not SOUND. Grounding (ADR-033 D7a): control overlap is pinned inline to the prompt's control list; the field-placement examples are corpus-independent. The live reads for risk linkage, persona scope, and mapping precedent depend on these corpus facts (verified 2026-09-30): controlComponentIdentityProvenance maps nist-ai-rmf MEASURE-2.7@1.0 (with MAP-3.4@1.0) and lists five personas (personaPlatformProvider, personaAgenticProvider, personaApplicationDeveloper, personaModelServing, personaGovernance); riskToolSourceProvenance's text says it typically manifests as riskRogueActions; riskToolRegistryTampering and riskRogueActions exist. Counterfactual design: the controlThirdPartyToolVettingProcess counterfactual states only the sound distinction between a one-time onboarding approval and an ongoing per-invocation runtime check; it deliberately makes no claim that the check is independent of vetting, since a per-call signature gate normally enforces the vetted set. The case tests that the critic does not over-dispute a sound counterfactual. A critic that confirms the distinction while asking that the vetting relation be stated as a dependency on the vetted set (the allowlist enforces what vetting approves) is behaving correctly; calling either counterfactual a strawman or recommending folding the draft into either fixture entry is not.
expectations: Uses only the fixture list provided in the prompt, not the live controls.yaml, to judge control-overlap/duplication (D7a) — but may and should still check the real risks.yaml/controls.yaml/components.yaml/personas.yaml for risk-linkage, mapping-precedent, and scope precision, since those are different corpus files from the one being fixture-pinned

Overall verdict is NEEDS-WORK — not SOUND (the draft is genuinely underspecified on at least one load-bearing point), and not RETHINK (the premise itself — a pre-invocation tool-identity gate — is not a duplicate of any fixture entry and is not fundamentally broken)

Every finding raised quotes specific draft text and cites specific, real corpus evidence (a risk's own wording, a real sibling control's mapping or persona list, a real component edge), or, for a field-placement finding, the design record (risk-map/docs/design/control-description-and-guidance.md), or, for a classical-fidelity finding, a named external standard or framework; a finding may also rest on another finding raised in the same review that is itself evidenced this way — none are vague, stylistic-only, or unsupported by a citation

Addresses both counterfactuals against the closest fixture entries (as SUPPORTED entries or as findings), and does not treat either counterfactual against the closest fixture entries (controlAgentActionAuthorizationGating, controlThirdPartyToolVettingProcess) as a strawman and does not recommend folding the draft into either; asking that the vetting relation be stated as a dependency on the vetted set (the allowlist enforces what vetting approves) is acceptable

At least one finding cites DG3, DG4, or DG5 of the design record, quotes the misplaced text in the draft's description (the signature/trust-root/signed-manifest mechanism, the negated means 'not a display name or free-text description', or the closing contrast with per-action authorization controls), and states where it belongs (guidance; for the contrast sentence, the boundary section of guidance)

Does not collapse into a pure altitude-check T1-T6 listing — findings are framed through the critic's own lenses (efficacy, altitude honesty, generalization, counterfactual quality) with its own tag taxonomy (SUPPORTED/WEAK/UNSUPPORTED/MISAPPLIED-ANALOGY/OVERREACH), not restated as raw altitude-check output

evals.prompt:

Title: Agent Prompt Injection Resilience
Description: Addresses prompt injection by ensuring the agent is aware that untrusted content may contain injected instructions.

expectations: Tags an efficacy finding UNSUPPORTED or WEAK on the claim that the control addresses prompt injection through the agent being 'aware' of injected instructions
Quotes the specific draft text ('ensuring the agent is aware that untrusted content may contain injected instructions') as the challenged claim
Explains that naming or being aware of a risk is not the same as reducing it, especially against a determined adversary
Overall verdict is NEEDS-WORK or RETHINK, not SOUND

evals.prompt:
Stress-test this draft control:

Title: Agent Action Policy Enforcement Point
Description: Implements a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) that intercepts every agent tool call and enforces access decisions using attribute-based access control (ABAC).

The draft does not describe where or how the access decision itself is made, and does not define any attributes or policies the ABAC model would evaluate against.
evals.expected_output: Tags a MISAPPLIED-ANALOGY finding: the draft invokes the PEP/ABAC reference architecture but omits the Policy Decision Point and the attribute/policy definitions that make the model coherent — an enforcement point with no decision point enforces nothing meaningful. Overall verdict NEEDS-WORK or RETHINK, not SOUND. Grounding (ADR-033 D7a): the prompt pins no fixture, so the critic reads the live corpus, which carries componentAuthorizationPolicyEnforcementPoint and componentAuthorizationPolicyDecisionPoint (PEP/PDP as components, citing NIST SP 800-162) and controlAgentPluginPermissions (least-privilege tool permissions with reference monitors), verified 2026-10-02. Against that corpus, a draft whose only content is 'implement a PEP' restates an existing component and overlaps an existing control, which the charter's RETHINK definition covers (duplicates an existing one); RETHINK on that quoted evidence is a correct outcome, not an over-escalation.
expectations: Tags a MISAPPLIED-ANALOGY finding on the PEP/ABAC framing
Identifies specifically what is missing for the analogy to be coherent: the Policy Decision Point (PDP) and the attribute/policy definitions ABAC requires
Quotes the draft's PEP/ABAC language as the specific text under challenge

Overall verdict is NEEDS-WORK or RETHINK, not SOUND, since a half-applied reference architecture is treated as a load-bearing weakness (RETHINK is acceptable where the critic cites the existing PEP/PDP components or controlAgentPluginPermissions as a duplicate)

Checks risk-map/yaml/components.yaml and cites the existing componentAuthorizationPolicyEnforcementPoint and/or componentAuthorizationPolicyDecisionPoint; does not propose modelling a policy enforcement point as a component as if none existed

expectations: Does not assert the identifier's validity or invalidity as a bare claim — shows evidence of genuine live-verification (an actual external/web check attempted or performed), not merely a local corpus-range heuristic; MITRE ATLAS never qualifies for the closed-and-unversioned live-verify exemption, so a comparison against corpus-observed id ranges alone is not sufficient evidence
States which audit-framework-mappings skill mode it used — candidate mode, since this draft control has no row in controls.yaml — and the entity type (control)

evals.prompt: Stress-test this proposed addition to the real, existing corpus control controlInputValidationAndSanitization (risk-map/yaml/controls.yaml — not a fixture): a PR proposes adding a fifth mitre-atlas mapping, AML.M0021@5.0.1, on the grounds that generative-AI guideline/guardrail-style prompt safety controls are a natural extension of this control's existing adversarial-query-blocking scope. Stress-test this proposed mapping addition.
evals.expected_output: Looks up controlInputValidationAndSanitization in the real, live controls.yaml and finds its current mitre-atlas mappings are AML.M0010@5.0.1, AML.M0015@5.0.1, AML.M0020@5.0.1, AML.M0024@5.0.1 — 4 total, not just the single proposed value. Confirms AML.M0021@5.0.1 (Generative AI Guidelines) is itself a real, current, correctly-classified mitigation (mitigation, not technique) — the candidate value's own currency and class are not the problem. Its relevance is not: ATLAS 5.0.1 defines M0021 as safety controls placed between user input and the model 'to help direct the model to produce desired outputs and prevent undesired outputs', 'implemented as instructions appended to all user prompts or as part of the instructions in the system prompt'; its technique-use text adds that 'model guidelines can instruct the model to refuse a response to unsafe inputs'. M0021 is therefore a mechanism of instructing the model, not of validating or filtering the input before it reaches the model. Implementing this control (block or restrict adversarial queries) neither implements nor contributes to writing model guidelines, so the addition fails the style guide's 'this control implements or contributes to this mitigation' test; the shared attack techniques (prompt injection, jailbreak) are not that test. The guardrail-style controls the PR invokes are AML.M0020 (Generative AI Guardrails: filters, validators, classifiers), which the control already carries; the PR conflates the two. Grounding: M0021 and M0020 definitions verified against mitre-atlas/atlas-data v5.0.1 data/mitigations.yaml on 2026-10-02. Independently, because the control already carries 4 mitre-atlas mappings, adding a fifth would push the framework's count to 5, exceeding the soft cap of 4 per risk-map/docs/contributing/framework-mappings-style-guide.md's selectivity rule — a finding only reachable by pulling the complete existing set from the corpus rather than evaluating the proposed value in isolation. States it used single-entity mode (entity type: control) since this is an existing corpus control, not a new draft. The style guide itself frames the soft cap as a prompt to re-examine, not a validation error; the relevance failure is what makes the addition one to reject, so the verdict is NEEDS-WORK or stricter, and the overshoot is still surfaced as its own finding.
expectations: Looks up the real, live risk-map/yaml/controls.yaml entry for controlInputValidationAndSanitization rather than evaluating the proposed AML.M0021@5.0.1 value in isolation

Names the specific existing mitre-atlas mappings it found on that control (AML.M0010@5.0.1, AML.M0015@5.0.1, AML.M0020@5.0.1, AML.M0024@5.0.1 — 4 total) as evidence the complete per-framework set was pulled, not just the single challenged value
Confirms AML.M0021@5.0.1 itself passes format/version and structural/class checks (a real, current, correctly-classed mitigation) — does not dispute the candidate value's own currency or class

Judges that the addition fails direct relevance, citing the ATLAS definition: M0021 works by instructing the model through prompt or system-prompt text (including instructions to refuse unsafe inputs), not by validating or filtering input, so this control does not implement or contribute to it; noting that the two share attack techniques is fine, and the guardrail-style controls the PR invokes are AML.M0020, which the control already carries
States which audit-framework-mappings skill mode it used — single-entity mode, since controlInputValidationAndSanitization already exists in controls.yaml — and names the entity type (control)

Concludes that adding this fifth value would push the framework's mapping count on this control to 5, exceeding the soft cap of 4, and explicitly surfaces this as a finding rather than silently ignoring it, citing risk-map/docs/contributing/framework-mappings-style-guide.md (not a skill) as the source of the soft-cap rule
Overall verdict is NEEDS-WORK or stricter, not SOUND
Recommends against adding the value (drop the addition); it does not approve it, with or without caveats

evals.prompt:
Novelty is settled for this request: overlap with the existing corpus has already been checked and no existing control covers this draft, so don't re-run or re-litigate it. Stress-test this draft control:

Title: Agent Outbound Destination Restriction
Description: Restrict the network destinations an agent can reach to those authorized for its current task, enforced at an HTTPS egress proxy. Unlike {{controlAgentPluginPermissions}}, which limits which tools an agent may invoke, this control governs where the agent's outbound traffic may go once a tool is running.
Guidance: Route agent-originated traffic through a policy-enforcing egress point that checks each destination against a per-agent allowlist derived from the task's declared needs, rather than relying on host firewall rules shared by every workload on the node.
Personas: personaAgenticProvider, personaApplicationDeveloper
Components: componentTools, componentOrchestrationOutputHandling
Risks: riskRogueActions, riskSensitiveDataDisclosure
evals.expected_output: Raises a field-placement finding on the description sentence 'Unlike {{controlAgentPluginPermissions}}, which limits which tools an agent may invoke, this control governs where the agent's outbound traffic may go once a tool is running.' It cites DG4 of the control description/guidance design record (risk-map/docs/design/control-description-and-guidance.md: `description` stands alone; no `{{control…}}` sentinel, and no sibling defined by contrast, in `description`) and routes the sentence to the boundary section of `guidance`, which is the last section, after the existing implementation paragraph. The 'HTTPS egress proxy' mention is a DG5 placement issue and may also be raised, but flagging it, or treating the sentinel sentence only as a protocol/generalization-honesty matter, does not satisfy the case: the shipped Generalization-honesty lens already catches a protocol name, and this case pins the DG4 citation and the boundary-section routing that it does not. Verdict is not SOUND (NEEDS-WORK expected). The critic returns the finding as a challenge for the author and does not rewrite the control. Grounding (ADR-033 D7a): corpus-independent. Novelty is a stipulated premise in the prompt (D7d), and the DG4 finding is judged from the draft text and the design record alone. Incidental corpus fact, not depended on: controlAgentPluginPermissions exists in risk-map/yaml/controls.yaml (verified 2026-09-30), so the sentinel resolves; an unresolved-sentinel finding, should that change, is additional to the DG4 finding, not a substitute for it.
expectations: Raises a finding that quotes the description sentence carrying {{controlAgentPluginPermissions}} and cites DG4 (from risk-map/docs/design/control-description-and-guidance.md) as the rule it breaks
Routes that sentence to the boundary section of `guidance` (the final section, after the implementation text) — not merely 'remove it' or 'reword it' within `description`

A response whose only placement-related finding is the protocol/mechanism mention ('HTTPS egress proxy') or a generic generalization-honesty point, without both the DG4 citation and the guidance-boundary routing for the sentinel sentence, fails this case
Does not rewrite the control; returns the finding as a challenge or required fix for the author
Overall verdict is not SOUND
